# GOAL — flutter_agent_harness

## Objective

Build the **ideal cross-platform AI agent harness in Dart**, ported from the
architecture of **pi-mono** (`packages/ai` + `packages/agent`), publishable on
pub.dev and runnable everywhere Dart runs: **VM, Flutter desktop, iOS/Android,
and web**. The core package must stay **pure Dart** — no `dart:io`, no Flutter
imports in `lib/` (platform specifics live behind abstractions).

This repo is the successor to the adk_dart-based assistant stack in the
`yoclip` project; once mature it will power the yoclip Studio AI assistant.

## Reference codebases (read these first)

### Primary architecture reference — pi-mono

`/Users/Uladzimir_Klyshevich/git/references/pi/`

- `packages/ai/` (~8.7k LOC TS) — provider adapters behind one contract:
  `stream(model, context, options) → AssistantMessageEventStream`.
  Study these files before writing any provider code:
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts` (~1205 LOC) — the
    canonical adapter; also covers OpenRouter (`baseUrl` swap, first-class).
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts` (~1242 LOC) — includes a
    hand-rolled SSE decoder at lines 260–409; port this to Dart.
  - `packages/ai/src/stream.ts` — event contract:
    `start → text/thinking/toolcall_{start,delta,end} → done|error`, every
    delta event carries the **live partial message** (partial-first design).
  - `packages/ai/src/utils/overflow.ts` — provider-specific context-overflow
    detection via error-message regexes.
  - **Invariant to preserve: providers never throw.** All failures —
    network, 429, abort, malformed SSE — arrive as an `error` event with
    `stopReason: error|aborted`. The agent loop never sees an exception from
    a provider.
- `packages/agent/` (~8.1k LOC TS):
  - `packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts` (748 LOC) — the low-level async loop;
    port its shape, not its incidental JS-isms.
  - `packages/agent/src/agent.ts` (557 LOC) — stateful `Agent` with
    **steering / follow-up queues** (inject user messages mid-run — this is
    first-class behavior we must keep) and hooks (`beforeToolCall`,
    `afterToolCall`, `transformContext`, `prepareNextTurn`).
  - session layer — sessions as an **append-only JSONL tree** of records
    (branching, labels). Flat linear history is not acceptable.
  - compaction pipeline (~760 LOC) — `estimateTokens` (chars/4 heuristic,
    images ≈ 1200 tokens) → `shouldCompact` (reserve 16384 tokens) →
    `findCutPoint` (keep ~20k recent tokens) → `generateSummary` via LLM with
    a fixed structured prompt. Token-based, never message-count-based.
  - `ExecutionEnv` abstraction (FileSystem + Shell) — our portability
    boundary: default implementation uses `dart:io`, a web implementation
----

GOAL.md is the repo roadmap — the "TTSR maxInjectionsPerTurn" reference in the PR description refers to some pattern (likely "Tool-The-Steer-Request" or a pi-mono concept). Not critical.

Now let me check AGENTS.md for review-relevant project conventions (line gates, test rules).

messages.preview: Let me verify formatting and check the PR description's claim about the yield token one more time, plus scan for any remaining issues in the diff.

blocks.text:
The handler subscribes to the main Agent's event stream (agent events). Subagent (task tool) runs execute inside the `task` tool executor with their own Agent — their tool events don't propagate to the parent's event stream. So the E3 claim holds: the parent tracker never sees child calls. Only the parent's own `task` TOOL call (which can run long) would be watched — and steering into the parent agent during a child's run: the `task` tool is yield-aware? If the parent's task tool gets soft-yielded, does the child get aborted or does it deliver at boundary? Not this PR's concern (same behavior as user steers today).

Now — the ONE remaining significant thread: the PR-description vs implementation contradiction on the yield token, and the related "because the user sent a message" misattribution. Let me nail down the exact behavior with the AC1 test's model: in AC1 the test uses `stuckCallFake()` whose bash goes through the mock `shell` (GatedShell) — the bash tool executes via the injected `Shell`. Is the yield token present in the test setup? The test's bash is executed through MemoryExecutionEnv's shell. The yield path requires `canJob && currentYieldToken() != null`. In the test env, jobs (ShellJobRegistry) exist? `canJob` depends on the jobs registry availability — with MemoryExecutionEnv, likely yes. Then bash runs via `_shellViaJob` — a job started, and `_awaitJobOutcome` awaits `entry.settled` vs `yieldToken.onCancel`. In the AC1 test the nudge fires while the call is in flight → yield token cancels → the bash result becomes "moved to background job … because the user sent a message"... but wait — the GatedShell gate hasn't released! `_shellViaJob` starts a JOB via `jobs.start(command, options)` — which runs the command through the Shell — the gate holds it. The yield fires → `_awaitJobOutcome` returns the "moved to background" result → the tool call ENDS (as a backgrounded job) → `toolCallEnded` → step boundary → nudge delivered. Then `shell.release()` — the test releases the gate so the job settles.

So in the test, the stuck call IS backgrounded by the nudge's steer. The test comment says: "Ending it lets the run reach the step boundary where the queued nudge delivers (the non-yield tool path; the yield-aware bash path backgrounds instead and delivers the same way)." — the comment acknowledges both paths exist. Which path runs depends on whether the shell/job registry is available.

Hmm OK wait, actually now I realize the AC1 test's `waitForIt(() => fake.calls >= 2, ...)` — after `shell.release()`. If the yield path backgrounded the call, the tool result arrives immediately at yield time WITHOUT `shell.release()`... then `fake.calls >= 2` would be satisfied before release. The test releases first, so either path converges. Fine.

So the definitive behavior: **when bash is yield-aware (jobs available — the normal CLI case), the watchdog nudge auto-backgrounds the stuck call at escalation time.** The notice text then says "This notice does not stop the call" and offers "keep waiting (continue as-is)" as option 1 — but the call has ALREADY been moved to background; "keep waiting" is moot for that call (though the backgrounded job keeps running, so "keep waiting" is still coherent in the sense of "let the job finish").

And the tool result text says "because the user sent a message" — false attribution to the user.

And the PR description says "the nudge ... never fires the yield token (the model must decide — soft-yield stays reserved for user steers)" — contradicted by the implementation.

Hmm, wait. Let me re-read the PR description ONE more time to be extra careful, because this is my headline finding:

No Python formatter enforced in AGENTS.md for bench/ — py_compile clean is the bar per the PR. The `progress_bytes=None if sample is None else len(...)` formatting is unusual but acceptable for bench code.

Now, let me re-read the notice text once more for the model-facing semantics:

```
<system-notice>
[liveness watchdog] Foreground tool call `bash` ("sleep 500") has been running 300s with no output. Decide and act on your next turn: keep waiting (continue as-is), background the work (`bash background: true` for a new command; a call already moved to the background is a job — manage it with bash_job action: output | status | stop), or kill the job. This notice does not stop the call.
</system-notice>
```

Interesting — the text says "a call already moved to the background is a job — manage it with bash_job" — this phrasing shows the AUTHOR knew the call may already be backgrounded (by the steer's yield). So the notice text is actually coherent with the yield behavior. The contradictory artifact is the PR DESCRIPTION ("never fires the yield token — soft-yield stays reserved for user steers") and, to a lesser degree, the tool-result text "because the user sent a message".

Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider the "keep waiting" option: for the yield-aware-bash case, the call gets backgrounded AT escalation. "Keep waiting (continue as-is)" would then be a no-op choice — the call is already a background job; the model can only wait for its settle notice. Not broken — the option list is generic.

So my headline finding stands but let me finalize severity: 
- Finding 1 (IMPORTANT): PR description explicitly claims "never fires the yield token / soft-yield stays reserved for user steers", but `_nudgeStuckCall` steers via `_agent.steer`, which fires the soft-yield token and auto-backgrounds a yield-aware bash at escalation time. The code comment + tests acknowledge this. The description (and ticket.md, same text) must be reconciled — a reviewer merging based on the description would believe a different behavior ships. Also the delivery-at-boundary claim "busy-gated so boundary delivery is the only path" is imprecise given the yield path delivers the tool result early.

Actually — hmm, is it possible the description means "never fires the yield token" = [REDACTED:Sensitive Value] cancels the run's main CancelToken (the abort token)? No — it says "soft-yield stays reserved for user steers", which is unambiguous: the soft-yield should fire only for user steers. The implementation fires it for watchdog steers. Clear contradiction.

- Finding 2 (IMPORTANT or SUGGESTION?): the tool result `_awaitJobOutcome` text "was moved to background job X ... because the user sent a message" — misattributes the watchdog nudge to the USER. The PR description itself claims "attribution prefix names the watchdog, not the user". The notice carries the watchdog attribution, but the tool result (which arrives FIRST in the transcript, directly after the tool call) tells the model the USER sent a message. This is model-facing misinformation about who intervened — in an agent harness whose whole point is honest attribution (the repo has extensive attribution discipline: "[from <id>]" mail prefixes, settle notices, etc.). BUT the machinery is pre-existing (job-settle steers have the same issue today). This PR extends it to a fully automatic, recurring trigger (every stuck call). I'll file it as IMPORTANT — suggest passing an attribution hint (e.g. a parameter on the yield cancel reason, or rewording to "because a steering message arrived") or at least acknowledging it.

Actually, let me check: `yieldSource.cancel('steering message arrived')` — the cancel reason string exists but `_awaitJobOutcome` ignores the reason and hard-codes "the user sent a message". The fix is trivial: use the cancel reason or a neutral wording. Good actionable suggestion.

- Finding 3 (SUGGESTION): `toolNudge` doc/comment staleness — `approval_commands.dart` comment "headless/line mode watch the foreground call... TUI mode is skipped inside" is now wrong (the gate was removed). Stale comment on an unchanged file — general comment material, not inline.

- Finding 4 (SUGGESTION): `liveness_bytes_of` counts `str.splitlines()` boundaries (splits on \r, \v, \f, \u2028, ...) and assumes +1 byte per line — CRLF pane output undercounts by 1 byte/line; a stream not ending in a newline overcounts by 1. Audit-visibility only; document or normalize to `\n` splits.

- Finding 5 (SUGGESTION): harbor `_write_audit` reads the whole pane stream via `cat` (up to tens of MB) and byte-counts by re-encoding decoded text — may disagree with the ladder's `wc -c` measurement for non-UTF-8 bytes; could reuse `wc -c` for progress_bytes and a grep-based count for liveness to avoid shipping the full stream through the exec channel.

- Finding 6 (SUGGESTION): `nudgeAnchor` duplicated in the test file instead of exported from lib (like toolLivenessEscalationHint); if the lib wording drifts, the test still passes on the duplicated literal — wait, no: if the LIB text changes, the test's `contains(nudgeAnchor)` uses the test's own const, so the test would keep passing even if lib dropped the anchor. The anchor is part of the delivery contract (the PR says "attribution prefix names the watchdog"); a lib-exported anchor would pin it. SUGGESTION.

- Finding 7 (SUGGESTION): `_nudgeStuckCall` spends the budget (`_nudgesLeft--`) before `steer` — if `steer` were a no-op (queue closed — not currently possible), the budget burns. Trivial; probably skip this one. Actually it's fine to skip.

- Finding 8: E2 cap const name `maxToolNudgesPerRun` vs semantics "per turn" (reset per user prompt; a REPL session runs many turns per RUN). The name says perRun, the docs say per turn. Naming inconsistency — SUGGESTION. Hmm: "Per-run cap on #1185 stuck-call nudges (E2...)" but the field doc says "Nudges left this turn... reset at every real turn start". In REPL, one RUN = many turns; the budget refills per turn, so the effective cap is per-turn. The const name is misleading. Minor SUGGESTION.

- Finding 9: the `_beginUserPrompt` refill skips auto-continue turns (intentional per the empty-reply-nudge precedent) but the PR description says "refills at each `_beginUserPrompt`" — imprecise. Fold into finding 1's description-vs-code reconciliation list.

Now — anything BLOCKING? Let me scan the checklist once more:

- Scope creep? The bench AC6 additions are in scope (the PR description declares them). The `cliFor` test-helper signature change is test-infrastructure for the new tests. OK.
- Security: no secrets handled; the nudge embeds tool detail (model's own command) into context — self-input; no shell interpolation anywhere (Dart side). The Python side: `printf %s {payload}` with payload = base64 (safe charset) — pre-existing pattern. No injection.
- Dead code / unused imports: the test file adds `import waiting_heartbeat.dart` (used for WaitingConfig). `dart analyze` clean on the PR branch except pre-existing infos. OK.
- Error paths: `_read_progress_stream` swallows (pattern-consistent). `_nudgeStuckCall` best-effort. OK.
- Tests: strong coverage — AC1/2/3/4/E2/E5 + formatter + config. Genuinely meaningful assertions (context inspection, JSONL persistence check). Good.
- Backward compat: config additive (new optional knob, strict-key list extended — unknown keys still rejected; someone with `toolNudge` in yaml before this PR would have failed, fine). `audit_dict` additive kwargs. `cliFor` is test-internal.
- CI safety: no workflow changes.

One more potential correctness issue to probe: **the tracker now arms in TUI mode — do the liveness reminders in TUI mode fire `onRemind` → early return → fine. But `callStarted` arms the timer chain in TUI. On abrupt TUI exit (Ctrl+C), `liveness.stop()` called?** If not, the timer fires post-exit → `_evaluate` → `onRemind` → `_cli._useTui` return; `onEscalate` → `_nudgeStuckCall` → `_cli._exited` return. Safe. And `toolCallEnded` removes calls → chain disarms. The pre-existing "timer chain can outlive the session by a tick" concern is guarded by the `_exited` checks. OK.

blocks.text:
# PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. Do NOT write `outputs/response.md`; the review is posted to GitHub only.

minutes — gh-71). These rules govern the verdict; every other instruction
(severity definitions, output files, thread etiquette) is unchanged.

## Verdict mapping

Classify findings exactly as instructed:

- 🚨 **BLOCKING** — correctness/bug findings: broken behavior, failing
  gates (red CI), scope violations, security issues, data loss.
- ⚠️ **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability debt worth fixing, but the PR
  works as shipped.
- 💡 **SUGGESTION** — style, wording, import order, dartdoc refs, polish.

Then map to the verdict:

| Findings | `recommendation` |
|---|---|
| Any 🚨 BLOCKING (correctness/bug) | `REQUEST_CHANGES` — or `BLOCK` for security / data loss |
| No 🚨 BLOCKING — only ⚠️ / 💡 remain | `APPROVE` |

`APPROVE` with remaining ⚠️/💡 findings is the expected terminal state
(`allowApproveWithSuggestions: true`): post every remaining finding as
before (inline threads + general comment) — they do **not** block the merge
and must **not** trigger another rework round.

## Anti-patterns (observed live, gh-71)

- ❌ Returning `REQUEST_CHANGES` because a re-review surfaced new
  suggestion-level nits (docs wording, import style, dartdoc refs). A cycle
  with only suggestion-level findings **must** converge to `APPROVE`.
- ❌ `REQUEST_CHANGES` while `issueCounts.blocking` is `0` — the machine
  treats that as an approval and skips the rework round. Keep
  `issueCounts` accurate: it is the machine's source of truth, not prose.
  The machine also cross-checks the counter against your inline comments
  (a `severity: "BLOCKING"` entry or a 🚨 marker in the referenced comment
  file) before honoring a blocking-0 approval — if any finding is truly
  blocking, set `recommendation: REQUEST_CHANGES` with `blocking: 1`+.
- ❌ Verdict-by-prose: never phrase the verdict only in the summary text.
  The `recommendation` field of `outputs/pr_review.json` is the verdict.
- ❌ Re-opening a thread that the rework demonstrably fixed in this diff —
  add its id to `resolvedThreadIds` instead.

## Label guard rails — the chore:pin lane (live: fa pr-1104, 2026-09-30)

`chore:pin` is a trusted, **non-exclusive** factory fast-lane: several PRs
may carry it at the same time (a release bump `chore/release-vX.Y.Z` AND a
factory pin `chore/factory-pin-*` are both legitimate holders — they ride
the lane independently). Reviews must therefore:

- ❌ **NEVER remove `chore:pin` from any PR** — not as a "one pin" dedup,
  not as a side-effect of closing a related PR as superseded. Removing it
  from the release bump stranded the v1.0.494 tag behind the guest queue
  for an hour (fa pr-1104, unlabeled 13:31:08Z while pr-1105 was closed).
- ✅ When a PR is superseded (e.g. a workflow change already shipped via
  another PR), close **only that PR** and leave every label on every other
  PR untouched. Label restoration is a keeper action, not yours.
- ✅ If you believe two `chore:pin` holders conflict, SAY SO in the review
  comment and keep both labels — the owner resolves the lane, the machine
  only merges.

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1187
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1187
- **Title**: feat(cli): stuck foreground tool calls nudge the model via steering (#1185)
- **Author**: vabhzw17eg2qu4m9-bit
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1185` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 10
- **Additions**: +610
- **Deletions**: -29
- **Created**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z

## PR Description

## What & why

A foreground tool call that outlasts `waiting.toolEscalateSeconds` today gets exactly one console hint (gh-1055) — and nothing else. In the TBench-1 evidence (run 36990604714, trial extract-moves-from-video) the agent's OCR heredoc ran 600+s silent while the liveness tracker printed `[WAIT] … background candidate …` to a headless container console the model can never read. The run burned its whole budget and died as `agent_timeout`.

## Root cause of the gap

`WaitingCoordinator.liveness.onEscalate` (agent_cli_waiting.dart) was wired to `_printLiveness` only: the escalation event never touched the agent loop. The steering channel (agent-level `steer()` → queue → step-boundary poll) already delivers mid-run messages to the model — the escalation simply didn't use it.

## Design

On escalation (once per stuck call, deduped in the tracker's `escalated` flag) the CLI now ALSO steers a system-notice message through the existing steering path: `[liveness watchdog] <tool> "<detail>" has been running Ns with no output — decide: keep waiting / bash background: true / kill it. The call is still running; this notice does not stop it.` Delivery is the standard boundary poll (persisted as a user message, same recovery semantics as user steers; attribution prefix names the watchdog, not the user). Safeguards per the GOAL: the nudge never stops/aborts the call and never fires the yield token (the model must decide — soft-yield stays reserved for user steers); E2 storm cap = 3 per turn (TTSR `maxInjectionsPerTurn` analog, refills at each `_beginUserPrompt`); busy-gated so boundary delivery is the only path; `waiting.toolNudge: false` kill switch (E5). Console output unchanged (non-goal). TUI runs arm the same watch — only the console lines stay TUI-gated (AC4). E3: child runs emit tool events only on their own Agent's stream, so a parent's tracker physically never sees a child call — a stuck child can only ever nudge its own session (by construction; no new mechanism added). Bench AC6: the #1122 audit (`bench/fa_agent_timeout.py`) now measures the harness-originated share of the progress sample (`[WAIT]` lines inside the pane byte stream) and records `progress_sample_bytes`/`liveness_bytes`/`progress_note` in `fa-agent-timeout.json` — both the harbor adapter (which runs the ladder) and tests updated. Related finding: `bench/terminal_bench/fa_agent.py`'s legacy watcher misses `_tap_pane`/`_progress_bytes`/`_write_audit` (its ladder path predates #1127's audit; crashes if ever run with knobs) — left as a separate follow-up, noted here for visibility.

## Verification

All commands run in `.worktrees/issue-1185` (Dart 3.13.4):

- `dart test test/cli/tool_liveness_test.dart test/cli/agent_cli_tool_liveness_test.dart` → **12 passed** — covers AC1 (ONE nudge steered, model's next request context contains it, session JSONL records it as a user message), AC2 (ladder extensions never re-nudge; a NEW stuck call gets its own single injection; AC3 same flag: no further injection, no forced kill), AC4 (TUI run nudges, console stays silent), E2 (4 distinct stuck calls → 3 nudges, refill next turn), E5 (`toolNudge: false` keeps the console line, drops the injection), plus nudge-formatter and yaml knob tests.
- `python3 -m unittest bench.terminal_bench.test_fa_agent_timeout` → **33 tests OK** (12 adapter legs skip: terminal_bench not installed) incl. new AC6 audit-measurement tests; `py_compile` clean on all touched bench files.
- `dart format` → clean (6 files, 2 changed). `dart analyze` → zero new issues (only the 3 pre-existing `prefer_initializing_formals` infos on untouched lines, byte-identical to HEAD).
- `dart test --exclude-tags integration` → 8538+ pass; the 24 failures are pre-existing sandbox/environment legs — verified byte-identical `+57 ~3 -5` on stashed clean HEAD for the suspect trio (waiting-integration, shell_job_io, io_execution_env); rest are PTY/macos-sandbox live legs this agent's sandbox SIGKILLs. The PTY/CLI-surface integration legs are covered by the nightly `test-integration` job (`dart test test/integration --exclude-tags llm,browser-ext,perf,pty`, ci.yml).

Fixes #1185

"""Unit tests for the bench agent-timeout ladder (issue #1122).

Run: python3 -m unittest discover -s bench/terminal_bench
The adapter-level tests skip when terminal_bench / harbor is not installed;
the ladder tests run anywhere (pure stdlib shared module).
"""
import asyncio
import base64
import importlib.util
import json
import os
import sys
import tempfile
import threading
import time
import types
import unittest
from pathlib import Path
from unittest import mock

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]))

import fa_agent_timeout
from fa_agent_timeout import ProgressLadder, TimeoutKnobs, audit_dict

def _importable(name: str) -> bool:
    # find_spec is not enough: with bench/terminal_bench on sys.path (as
    # unittest discover does), find_spec("terminal_bench") matches the
    # DIRECTORY itself as a namespace package and false-positives.
    try:
        importlib.import_module(name)
        return True
    except ImportError:
        return False


TB_AVAILABLE = _importable("terminal_bench.agents.base_agent")
HARBOR_AVAILABLE = _importable("harbor")

KNOB_NAMES = (
    "FA_AGENT_TIMEOUT_SEC",
    "FA_PROGRESS_EXTENSION",
    "FA_AGENT_IDLE_WINDOW_SEC",
    "FA_AGENT_CEILING_MULTIPLIER",
)


def clean_env(**overrides):
    env = {name: value for name, value in os.environ.items() if name not in KNOB_NAMES}
    env.update(overrides)
    return env


class KnobParsingTest(unittest.TestCase):
    """UT-1 / AC3: input plumbing — absent = no takeover, flag = effective cap."""

    def test_absent_knobs_means_no_takeover(self):
        self.assertIsNone(TimeoutKnobs.from_env(clean_env()))

Now let me continue the deeper review. Remaining areas to examine:

1. **The contradiction between the PR description ("never fires the yield token") and the implementation (`_agent.steer` fires soft-yield → yield-aware bash auto-backgrounded)** — plus the notice text "This notice does not stop the call" being misleading in the yield-aware path, and the tool-result text "because the user sent a message" misattributing the watchdog to the user.

Wait — actually let me think again about whether the yield token fires for a FOREGROUND stuck bash. The scenario: model calls bash (foreground). The bash tool, when jobs are available and yield token exists, runs via `_shellViaJob` (job from the start, awaited inline). Watchdog escalates at 300s → `_agent.steer(...)` → enqueue → `onEnqueue` → `_steeringArrived.add(null)` → the tool phase's `notificationSub` fires → `yieldSource.cancel('steering message arrived')` → `_awaitJobOutcome`'s `Future.any` sees `yieldToken.onCancel` first → returns "moved to background job X ... because the user sent a message". So yes — the stuck foreground bash is IMMEDIATELY backgrounded by the watchdog's steer, not by the model's decision.

Is that the intended design? The PR description says NO ("never fires the yield token... soft-yield stays reserved for user steers"), the code comment says YES ("so a stuck yield-aware bash moves to a background job"). And the AC1 test comment acknowledges "the yield-aware bash path backgrounds instead and delivers the same way". # GOAL — flutter_agent_harness

## Objective

Build the **ideal cross-platform AI agent harness in Dart**, ported from the
architecture of **pi-mono** (`packages/ai` + `packages/agent`), publishable on
pub.dev and runnable everywhere Dart runs: **VM, Flutter desktop, iOS/Android,
and web**. The core package must stay **pure Dart** — no `dart:io`, no Flutter
imports in `lib/` (platform specifics live behind abstractions).

This repo is the successor to the adk_dart-based assistant stack in the
`yoclip` project; once mature it will power the yoclip Studio AI assistant.

## Reference codebases (read these first)

### Primary architecture reference — pi-mono

`/Users/Uladzimir_Klyshevich/git/references/pi/`

- `packages/ai/` (~8.7k LOC TS) — provider adapters behind one contract:
  `stream(model, context, options) → AssistantMessageEventStream`.
  Study these files before writing any provider code:
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts` (~1205 LOC) — the
    canonical adapter; also covers OpenRouter (`baseUrl` swap, first-class).
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts` (~1242 LOC) — includes a
    hand-rolled SSE decoder at lines 260–409; port this to Dart.
  - `packages/ai/src/stream.ts` — event contract:
    `start → text/thinking/toolcall_{start,delta,end} → done|error`, every
    delta event carries the **live partial message** (partial-first design).
  - `packages/ai/src/utils/overflow.ts` — provider-specific context-overflow
    detection via error-message regexes.
  - **Invariant to preserve: providers never throw.** All failures —
    network, 429, abort, malformed SSE — arrive as an `error` event with
    `stopReason: error|aborted`. The agent loop never sees an exception from
    a provider.
- `packages/agent/` (~8.1k LOC TS):
  - `packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts` (748 LOC) — the low-level async loop;
    port its shape, not its incidental JS-isms.
  - `packages/agent/src/agent.ts` (557 LOC) — stateful `Agent` with
    **steering / follow-up queues** (inject user messages mid-run — this is
    first-class behavior we must keep) and hooks (`beforeToolCall`,
    `afterToolCall`, `transformContext`, `prepareNextTurn`).
  - session layer — sessions as an **append-only JSONL tree** of records
    (branching, labels). Flat linear history is not acceptable.
  - compaction pipeline (~760 LOC) — `estimateTokens` (chars/4 heuristic,
    images ≈ 1200 tokens) → `shouldCompact` (reserve 16384 tokens) →
    `findCutPoint` (keep ~20k recent tokens) → `generateSummary` via LLM with
    a fixed structured prompt. Token-based, never message-count-based.
  - `ExecutionEnv` abstraction (FileSystem + Shell) — our portability
    boundary: default implementation uses `dart:io`, a web implementation
----

GOAL.md is the repo roadmap — the "TTSR maxInjectionsPerTurn" reference in the PR description refers to some pattern (likely "Tool-The-Steer-Request" or a pi-mono concept). Not critical.

blocks.text:
# PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. Do NOT write `outputs/response.md`; the review is posted to GitHub only.

blocks.text:
# Review verdict rules — machine protocol (binding)

The review↔rework loop is a machine, not a conversation: your
`recommendation` in `outputs/pr_review.json` is parsed mechanically and
drives issue labels, rework runs and CI (each wasted round costs 15–20 CI
minutes — gh-71). These rules govern the verdict; every other instruction
(severity definitions, output files, thread etiquette) is unchanged.

## Verdict mapping

Classify findings exactly as instructed:

- 🚨 **BLOCKING** — correctness/bug findings: broken behavior, failing
  gates (red CI), scope violations, security issues, data loss.
- ⚠️ **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability debt worth fixing, but the PR
  works as shipped.
- 💡 **SUGGESTION** — style, wording, import order, dartdoc refs, polish.

Then map to the verdict:

| Findings | `recommendation` |
|---|---|
| Any 🚨 BLOCKING (correctness/bug) | `REQUEST_CHANGES` — or `BLOCK` for security / data loss |
| No 🚨 BLOCKING — only ⚠️ / 💡 remain | `APPROVE` |

`APPROVE` with remaining ⚠️/💡 findings is the expected terminal state
(`allowApproveWithSuggestions: true`): post every remaining finding as
before (inline threads + general comment) — they do **not** block the merge
and must **not** trigger another rework round.

## Anti-patterns (observed live, gh-71)

- ❌ Returning `REQUEST_CHANGES` because a re-review surfaced new
  suggestion-level nits (docs wording, import style, dartdoc refs). A cycle
  with only suggestion-level findings **must** converge to `APPROVE`.
- ❌ `REQUEST_CHANGES` while `issueCounts.blocking` is `0` — the machine
  treats that as an approval and skips the rework round. Keep
  `issueCounts` accurate: it is the machine's source of truth, not prose.
  The machine also cross-checks the counter against your inline comments
  (a `severity: "BLOCKING"` entry or a 🚨 marker in the referenced comment
  file) before honoring a blocking-0 approval — if any finding is truly
  blocking, set `recommendation: REQUEST_CHANGES` with `blocking: 1`+.
- ❌ Verdict-by-prose: never phrase the verdict only in the summary text.
  The `recommendation` field of `outputs/pr_review.json` is the verdict.
- ❌ Re-opening a thread that the rework demonstrably fixed in this diff —
  add its id to `resolvedThreadIds` instead.

## Label guard rails — the chore:pin lane (live: fa pr-1104, 2026-09-30)

`chore:pin` is a trusted, **non-exclusive** factory fast-lane: several PRs
may carry it at the same time (a release bump `chore/release-vX.Y.Z` AND a
factory pin `chore/factory-pin-*` are both legitimate holders — they ride
the lane independently). Reviews must therefore:

- ❌ **NEVER remove `chore:pin` from any PR** — not as a "one pin" dedup,
  not as a side-effect of closing a related PR as superseded. Removing it
  from the release bump stranded the v1.0.494 tag behind the guest queue
  for an hour (fa pr-1104, unlabeled 13:31:08Z while pr-1105 was closed).
- ✅ When a PR is superseded (e.g. a workflow change already shipped via
  another PR), close **only that PR** and leave every label on every other
  PR untouched. Label restoration is a keeper action, not yours.

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1187
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1187
- **Title**: feat(cli): stuck foreground tool calls nudge the model via steering (#1185)
- **Author**: vabhzw17eg2qu4m9-bit
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1185` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 10
- **Additions**: +610
- **Deletions**: -29
- **Created**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z

## PR Description

## What & why

A foreground tool call that outlasts `waiting.toolEscalateSeconds` today gets exactly one console hint (gh-1055) — and nothing else. In the TBench-1 evidence (run 36990604714, trial extract-moves-from-video) the agent's OCR heredoc ran 600+s silent while the liveness tracker printed `[WAIT] … background candidate …` to a headless container console the model can never read. The run burned its whole budget and died as `agent_timeout`.

## Root cause of the gap

`WaitingCoordinator.liveness.onEscalate` (agent_cli_waiting.dart) was wired to `_printLiveness` only: the escalation event never touched the agent loop. The steering channel (agent-level `steer()` → queue → step-boundary poll) already delivers mid-run messages to the model — the escalation simply didn't use it.

## Design

On escalation (once per stuck call, deduped in the tracker's `escalated` flag) the CLI now ALSO steers a system-notice message through the existing steering path: `[liveness watchdog] <tool> "<detail>" has been running Ns with no output — decide: keep waiting / bash background: true / kill it. The call is still running; this notice does not stop it.` Delivery is the standard boundary poll (persisted as a user message, same recovery semantics as user steers; attribution prefix names the watchdog, not the user). Safeguards per the GOAL: the nudge never stops/aborts the call and never fires the yield token (the model must decide — soft-yield stays reserved for user steers); E2 storm cap = 3 per turn (TTSR `maxInjectionsPerTurn` analog, refills at each `_beginUserPrompt`); busy-gated so boundary delivery is the only path; `waiting.toolNudge: false` kill switch (E5). Console output unchanged (non-goal). TUI runs arm the same watch — only the console lines stay TUI-gated (AC4). E3: child runs emit tool events only on their own Agent's stream, so a parent's tracker physically never sees a child call — a stuck child can only ever nudge its own session (by construction; no new mechanism added). Bench AC6: the #1122 audit (`bench/fa_agent_timeout.py`) now measures the harness-originated share of the progress sample (`[WAIT]` lines inside the pane byte stream) and records `progress_sample_bytes`/`liveness_bytes`/`progress_note` in `fa-agent-timeout.json` — both the harbor adapter (which runs the ladder) and tests updated. Related finding: `bench/terminal_bench/fa_agent.py`'s legacy watcher misses `_tap_pane`/`_progress_bytes`/`_write_audit` (its ladder path predates #1127's audit; crashes if ever run with knobs) — left as a separate follow-up, noted here for visibility.

## Verification

All commands run in `.worktrees/issue-1185` (Dart 3.13.4):

- `dart test test/cli/tool_liveness_test.dart test/cli/agent_cli_tool_liveness_test.dart` → **12 passed** — covers AC1 (ONE nudge steered, model's next request context contains it, session JSONL records it as a user message), AC2 (ladder extensions never re-nudge; a NEW stuck call gets its own single injection; AC3 same flag: no further injection, no forced kill), AC4 (TUI run nudges, console stays silent), E2 (4 distinct stuck calls → 3 nudges, refill next turn), E5 (`toolNudge: false` keeps the console line, drops the injection), plus nudge-formatter and yaml knob tests.
- `python3 -m unittest bench.terminal_bench.test_fa_agent_timeout` → **33 tests OK** (12 adapter legs skip: terminal_bench not installed) incl. new AC6 audit-measurement tests; `py_compile` clean on all touched bench files.
- `dart format` → clean (6 files, 2 changed). `dart analyze` → zero new issues (only the 3 pre-existing `prefer_initializing_formals` infos on untouched lines, byte-identical to HEAD).
- `dart test --exclude-tags integration` → 8538+ pass; the 24 failures are pre-existing sandbox/environment legs — verified byte-identical `+57 ~3 -5` on stashed clean HEAD for the suspect trio (waiting-integration, shell_job_io, io_execution_env); rest are PTY/macos-sandbox live legs this agent's sandbox SIGKILLs. The PTY/CLI-surface integration legs are covered by the nightly `test-integration` job (`dart test test/integration --exclude-tags llm,browser-ext,perf,pty`, ci.yml).

Fixes #1185

> /// MODEL through the steering channel — decide: keep waiting, background

>       'true` for a new command; a call already moved to the background is '
>       'a job — manage it with bash_job action: output | status | stop), or '

The bash tool, when jobs are available and yield token exists, runs via `_shellViaJob` (job from the start, awaited inline). Watchdog escalates at 300s → `_agent.steer(...)` → enqueue → `onEnqueue` → `_steeringArrived.add(null)` → the tool phase's `notificationSub` fires → `yieldSource.cancel('steering message arrived')` → `_awaitJobOutcome`'s `Future.any` sees `yieldToken.onCancel` first → returns "moved to background job X ... because the user sent a message". So yes — the stuck foreground bash is IMMEDIATELY backgrounded by the watchdog's steer, not by the model's decision.

# GOAL — flutter_agent_harness

## Objective

Build the **ideal cross-platform AI agent harness in Dart**, ported from the
architecture of **pi-mono** (`packages/ai` + `packages/agent`), publishable on
pub.dev and runnable everywhere Dart runs: **VM, Flutter desktop, iOS/Android,
and web**. The core package must stay **pure Dart** — no `dart:io`, no Flutter
imports in `lib/` (platform specifics live behind abstractions).

This repo is the successor to the adk_dart-based assistant stack in the
`yoclip` project; once mature it will power the yoclip Studio AI assistant.

## Reference codebases (read these first)

### Primary architecture reference — pi-mono

`/Users/Uladzimir_Klyshevich/git/references/pi/`

- `packages/ai/` (~8.7k LOC TS) — provider adapters behind one contract:
  `stream(model, context, options) → AssistantMessageEventStream`.
  Study these files before writing any provider code:
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts` (~1205 LOC) — the
    canonical adapter; also covers OpenRouter (`baseUrl` swap, first-class).
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts` (~1242 LOC) — includes a
    hand-rolled SSE decoder at lines 260–409; port this to Dart.
  - `packages/ai/src/stream.ts` — event contract:
    `start → text/thinking/toolcall_{start,delta,end} → done|error`, every
    delta event carries the **live partial message** (partial-first design).
  - `packages/ai/src/utils/overflow.ts` — provider-specific context-overflow
    detection via error-message regexes.
  - **Invariant to preserve: providers never throw.** All failures —
    network, 429, abort, malformed SSE — arrive as an `error` event with
    `stopReason: error|aborted`. The agent loop never sees an exception from
    a provider.
- `packages/agent/` (~8.1k LOC TS):
  - `packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts` (748 LOC) — the low-level async loop;
    port its shape, not its incidental JS-isms.
  - `packages/agent/src/agent.ts` (557 LOC) — stateful `Agent` with
    **steering / follow-up queues** (inject user messages mid-run — this is
    first-class behavior we must keep) and hooks (`beforeToolCall`,
    `afterToolCall`, `transformContext`, `prepareNextTurn`).
  - session layer — sessions as an **append-only JSONL tree** of records
    (branching, labels). Flat linear history is not acceptable.
  - compaction pipeline (~760 LOC) — `estimateTokens` (chars/4 heuristic,
    images ≈ 1200 tokens) → `shouldCompact` (reserve 16384 tokens) →
    `findCutPoint` (keep ~20k recent tokens) → `generateSummary` via LLM with
    a fixed structured prompt. Token-based, never message-count-based.
  - `ExecutionEnv` abstraction (FileSystem + Shell) — our portability
    boundary: default implementation uses `dart:io`, a web implementation
----

blocks.text:
# PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. Do NOT write `outputs/response.md`; the review is posted to GitHub only.

blocks.text:
# Review verdict rules — machine protocol (binding)

The review↔rework loop is a machine, not a conversation: your
`recommendation` in `outputs/pr_review.json` is parsed mechanically and
drives issue labels, rework runs and CI (each wasted round costs 15–20 CI
minutes — gh-71). These rules govern the verdict; every other instruction
(severity definitions, output files, thread etiquette) is unchanged.

## Verdict mapping

Classify findings exactly as instructed:

- 🚨 **BLOCKING** — correctness/bug findings: broken behavior, failing
  gates (red CI), scope violations, security issues, data loss.
- ⚠️ **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability debt worth fixing, but the PR
  works as shipped.
- 💡 **SUGGESTION** — style, wording, import order, dartdoc refs, polish.

Then map to the verdict:

| Findings | `recommendation` |
|---|---|
| Any 🚨 BLOCKING (correctness/bug) | `REQUEST_CHANGES` — or `BLOCK` for security / data loss |
| No 🚨 BLOCKING — only ⚠️ / 💡 remain | `APPROVE` |

`APPROVE` with remaining ⚠️/💡 findings is the expected terminal state
(`allowApproveWithSuggestions: true`): post every remaining finding as
before (inline threads + general comment) — they do **not** block the merge
and must **not** trigger another rework round.

## Anti-patterns (observed live, gh-71)

- ❌ Returning `REQUEST_CHANGES` because a re-review surfaced new
  suggestion-level nits (docs wording, import style, dartdoc refs). A cycle
  with only suggestion-level findings **must** converge to `APPROVE`.

# Pull Request Information

- **PR #**: 1187
- **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1187
- **Title**: feat(cli): stuck foreground tool calls nudge the model via steering (#1185)
- **Author**: vabhzw17eg2qu4m9-bit
- **Branch**: `ai/gh-1185` → `main`
- **State**: open
- **Files Changed**: 10
- **Additions**: +610
- **Deletions**: -29
- **Created**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z
- **Updated**: 2026-10-02T12:18:17Z

## PR Description

## What & why

A foreground tool call that outlasts `waiting.toolEscalateSeconds` today gets exactly one console hint (gh-1055) — and nothing else. In the TBench-1 evidence (run 36990604714, trial extract-moves-from-video) the agent's OCR heredoc ran 600+s silent while the liveness tracker printed `[WAIT] … background candidate …` to a headless container console the model can never read. The run burned its whole budget and died as `agent_timeout`.

## Root cause of the gap

`WaitingCoordinator.liveness.onEscalate` (agent_cli_waiting.dart) was wired to `_printLiveness` only: the escalation event never touched the agent loop. The steering channel (agent-level `steer()` → queue → step-boundary poll) already delivers mid-run messages to the model — the escalation simply didn't use it.

## Design

On escalation (once per stuck call, deduped in the tracker's `escalated` flag) the CLI now ALSO steers a system-notice message through the existing steering path: `[liveness watchdog] <tool> "<detail>" has been running Ns with no output — decide: keep waiting / bash background: true / kill it. The call is still running; this notice does not stop it.` Delivery is the standard boundary poll (persisted as a user message, same recovery semantics as user steers; attribution prefix names the watchdog, not the user). Safeguards per the GOAL: the nudge never stops/aborts the call and never fires the yield token (the model must decide — soft-yield stays reserved for user steers); E2 storm cap = 3 per turn (TTSR `maxInjectionsPerTurn` analog, refills at each `_beginUserPrompt`); busy-gated so boundary delivery is the only path; `waiting.toolNudge: false` kill switch (E5). Console output unchanged (non-goal). TUI runs arm the same watch — only the console lines stay TUI-gated (AC4). E3: child runs emit tool events only on their own Agent's stream, so a parent's tracker physically never sees a child call — a stuck child can only ever nudge its own session (by construction; no new mechanism added). Bench AC6: the #1122 audit (`bench/fa_agent_timeout.py`) now measures the harness-originated share of the progress sample (`[WAIT]` lines inside the pane byte stream) and records `progress_sample_bytes`/`liveness_bytes`/`progress_note` in `fa-agent-timeout.json` — both the harbor adapter (which runs the ladder) and tests updated. Related finding: `bench/terminal_bench/fa_agent.py`'s legacy watcher misses `_tap_pane`/`_progress_bytes`/`_write_audit` (its ladder path predates #1127's audit; crashes if ever run with knobs) — left as a separate follow-up, noted here for visibility.

## Verification

All commands run in `.worktrees/issue-1185` (Dart 3.13.4):

- `dart test test/cli/tool_liveness_test.dart test/cli/agent_cli_tool_liveness_test.dart` → **12 passed** — covers AC1 (ONE nudge steered, model's next request context contains it, session JSONL records it as a user message), AC2 (ladder extensions never re-nudge; a NEW stuck call gets its own single injection; AC3 same flag: no further injection, no forced kill), AC4 (TUI run nudges, console stays silent), E2 (4 distinct stuck calls → 3 nudges, refill next turn), E5 (`toolNudge: false` keeps the console line, drops the injection), plus nudge-formatter and yaml knob tests.
- `python3 -m unittest bench.terminal_bench.test_fa_agent_timeout` → **33 tests OK** (12 adapter legs skip: terminal_bench not installed) incl. new AC6 audit-measurement tests; `py_compile` clean on all touched bench files.
- `dart format` → clean (6 files, 2 changed). `dart analyze` → zero new issues (only the 3 pre-existing `prefer_initializing_formals` infos on untouched lines, byte-identical to HEAD).
- `dart test --exclude-tags integration` → 8538+ pass; the 24 failures are pre-existing sandbox/environment legs — verified byte-identical `+57 ~3 -5` on stashed clean HEAD for the suspect trio (waiting-integration, shell_job_io, io_execution_env); rest are PTY/macos-sandbox live legs this agent's sandbox SIGKILLs. The PTY/CLI-surface integration legs are covered by the nightly `test-integration` job (`dart test test/integration --exclude-tags llm,browser-ext,perf,pty`, ci.yml).

Fixes #1185

+def liveness_bytes_of(stream: str | bytes | None) -> int | None:

void _nudgeStuckCall(ToolLivenessCall call) {

# GOAL — flutter_agent_harness

## Objective

Build the **ideal cross-platform AI agent harness in Dart**, ported from the
architecture of **pi-mono** (`packages/ai` + `packages/agent`), publishable on
pub.dev and runnable everywhere Dart runs: **VM, Flutter desktop, iOS/Android,
and web**. The core package must stay **pure Dart** — no `dart:io`, no Flutter
imports in `lib/` (platform specifics live behind abstractions).

This repo is the successor to the adk_dart-based assistant stack in the
`yoclip` project; once mature it will power the yoclip Studio AI assistant.

## Reference codebases (read these first)

### Primary architecture reference — pi-mono

`/Users/Uladzimir_Klyshevich/git/references/pi/`

- `packages/ai/` (~8.7k LOC TS) — provider adapters behind one contract:
  `stream(model, context, options) → AssistantMessageEventStream`.
  Study these files before writing any provider code:
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts` (~1205 LOC) — the
    canonical adapter; also covers OpenRouter (`baseUrl` swap, first-class).
  - `packages/ai/src/providers/anthropic.ts` (~1242 LOC) — includes a
    hand-rolled SSE decoder at lines 260–409; port this to Dart.
  - `packages/ai/src/stream.ts` — event contract:
    `start → text/thinking/toolcall_{start,delta,end} → done|error`, every
    delta event carries the **live partial message** (partial-first design).
  - `packages/ai/src/utils/overflow.ts` — provider-specific context-overflow
    detection via error-message regexes.
  - **Invariant to preserve: providers never throw.** All failures —
    network, 429, abort, malformed SSE — arrive as an `error` event with
    `stopReason: error|aborted`. The agent loop never sees an exception from
    a provider.
- `packages/agent/` (~8.1k LOC TS):
  - `packages/agent/src/agent-loop.ts` (748 LOC) — the low-level async loop;
    port its shape, not its incidental JS-isms.
  - `packages/agent/src/agent.ts` (557 LOC) — stateful `Agent` with
    **steering / follow-up queues** (inject user messages mid-run — this is
    first-class behavior we must keep) and hooks (`beforeToolCall`,
    `afterToolCall`, `transformContext`, `prepareNextTurn`).
  - session layer — sessions as an **append-only JSONL tree** of records
    (branching, labels). Flat linear history is not acceptable.
  - compaction pipeline (~760 LOC) — `estimateTokens` (chars/4 heuristic,
    images ≈ 1200 tokens) → `shouldCompact` (reserve 16384 tokens) →
    `findCutPoint` (keep ~20k recent tokens) → `generateSummary` via LLM with
    a fixed structured prompt. Token-based, never message-count-based.
  - `ExecutionEnv` abstraction (FileSystem + Shell) — our portability
    boundary: default implementation uses `dart:io`, a web implementation
----

GOAL.md is the repo roadmap — the "TTSR maxInjectionsPerTurn" reference in the PR description refers to some pattern (likely "Tool-The-Steer-Request" or a pi-mono concept). Not critical.

blocks.text:
# PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,
pr_diff.txt, pr_files.txt, ci_failures.md,
ci_failures_full.log, pr_discussions.md,
pr_discussions_raw.json"] READ --> DIFF["2. Run diff checklist on pr_diff.txt"] DIFF --> FILES["3. Read full content of every changed file"] FILES --> CODEGRAPH["4. Use CodeGraph:
callers/callees of changed symbols,
search for sensitive patterns,
impact analysis"] CODEGRAPH --> DIMS["5. Evaluate review dimensions:
Security · Architecture/OOP · Code quality
Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. If `pr_diff.txt` is truncated, run `git diff origin/{baseBranch}...HEAD` to locate the correct line numbers. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. Do NOT write `outputs/response.md`; the review is posted to GitHub only.

# Review verdict rules — machine protocol (binding)

The review↔rework loop is a machine, not a conversation: your
`recommendation` in `outputs/pr_review.json` is parsed mechanically and
drives issue labels, rework runs and CI (each wasted round costs 15–20 CI
minutes — gh-71). These rules govern the verdict; every other instruction
(severity definitions, output files, thread etiquette) is unchanged.

## Verdict mapping

Classify findings exactly as instructed:

- 🚨 **BLOCKING** — correctness/bug findings: broken behavior, failing
  gates (red CI), scope violations, security issues, data loss.
- ⚠️ **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability debt worth fixing, but the PR
  works as shipped.
- 💡 **SUGGESTION** — style, wording, import order, dartdoc refs, polish.

Then map to the verdict:

| Findings | `recommendation` |
|---|---|
| Any 🚨 BLOCKING (correctness/bug) | `REQUEST_CHANGES` — or `BLOCK` for security / data loss |
| No 🚨 BLOCKING — only ⚠️ / 💡 remain | `APPROVE` |

`APPROVE` with remaining ⚠️/💡 findings is the expected terminal state
(`allowApproveWithSuggestions: true`): post every remaining finding as
before (inline threads + general comment) — they do **not** block the merge
and must **not** trigger another rework round.

## Anti-patterns (observed live, gh-71)

- ❌ Returning `REQUEST_CHANGES` because a re-review surfaced new
  suggestion-level nits (docs wording, import style, dartdoc refs). A cycle
  with only suggestion-level findings **must** converge to `APPROVE`.
- ❌ `REQUEST_CHANGES` while `issueCounts.blocking` is `0` — the machine
  treats that as an approval and skips the rework round. Keep
  `issueCounts` accurate: it is the machine's source of truth, not prose.
  The machine also cross-checks the counter against your inline comments
  (a `severity: "BLOCKING"` entry or a 🚨 marker in the referenced comment
  file) before honoring a blocking-0 approval — if any finding is truly
  blocking, set `recommendation: REQUEST_CHANGES` with `blocking: 1`+.
- ❌ Verdict-by-prose: never phrase the verdict only in the summary text.
  The `recommendation` field of `outputs/pr_review.json` is the verdict.
- ❌ Re-opening a thread that the rework demonstrably fixed in this diff —
  add its id to `resolvedThreadIds` instead.

## Label guard rails — the chore:pin lane (live: fa pr-1104, 2026-09-30)

`chore:pin` is a trusted, **non-exclusive** factory fast-lane: several PRs
may carry it at the same time (a release bump `chore/release-vX.Y.Z` AND a
factory pin `chore/factory-pin-*` are both legitimate holders — they ride
the lane independently). Reviews must therefore:

- ❌ **NEVER remove `chore:pin` from any PR** — not as a "one pin" dedup,
  not as a side-effect of closing a related PR as superseded. Removing it
  from the release bump stranded the v1.0.494 tag behind the guest queue
  for an hour (fa pr-1104, unlabeled 13:31:08Z while pr-1105 was closed).
- ✅ When a PR is superseded (e.g. a workflow change already shipped via
  another PR), close **only that PR** and leave every label on every other
  PR untouched. Label restoration is a keeper action, not yours.
- ✅ If you believe two `chore:pin` holders conflict, SAY SO in the review
  comment and keep both labels — the owner resolves the lane, the machine
  only merges.

# GitHub tracker comment

Use GitHub-flavored Markdown in `outputs/response.md` for GitHub issue
comments and descriptions. Your output is posted to the issue as-is — every
construct must render natively on GitHub.

- Headings: `##`, `###`
- Bullets: `- item`
- Numbered lists: `1. item`
- Bold: `**text**`
- Inline code: `` `code` ``
- Code block: ` ```lang ... ``` ` with a language tag (`dart`, `bash`, `json`)
- Link: `[text](url)`
- Tables: standard GFM table syntax (`|---|` separator row)

Do not use Jira wiki markup in GitHub fields: no `{code}...{code}` blocks,
no `{panel}` macros, no `h1.`/`h2.`/`h3.` heading prefixes, no
`{{monospace}}` inline code, no `[title|url]` links. None of it renders on
GitHub — a comment full of `{code}` fences and `h3.` headers is unreadable.

**IMPORTANT** When the issue references a parent story or related issues,
get them for full context using: `dmtools github_get_issue OWNER/REPO#NUMBER`
(the composite key form works directly).
